summary: Arabic chooses the negator by the kind of sentence and by the tense. A present verb is negated with لَا right before it: لَا أُحِبُّ الشَّايَ (I don’t like tea). A sentence without a verb (“is not”, “is not here”, “does not have”) is negated with لَيْسَ — a verb with past-tense endings but present meaning, which agrees with the subject (لَسْتُ، لَيْسَتْ، لَسْنَا …) and puts a noun or adjective predicate in the accusative: هٰذَا لَيْسَ شَايًا; لَيْسَ عِنْدِي مَاءٌ. “No / not any” (I have no water) is said by negating the sentence: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي مَاءٌ; “there is no …” can also be لَا + a noun in -a without tanwīn (لَا شَكَّ, no doubt). Nothing = لَا شَيْءَ, nobody = لَا أَحَدَ, and with a verb لَا … شَيْئًا (not … anything); never = لَا … أَبَدًا; neither … nor = لَا … وَلَا … . One negation per clause is enough: the verb is negated, and “anything / anyone” after it stays a plain indefinite (لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا). The past is negated with لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ آكُلْ), the future with لَنْ + subjunctive (لَنْ آكُلَ); مَا + past is classical and dialectal — these come with the past and the future. The answer “no” is also لَا.

askYourself: Is there a present verb? → لَا directly before it; the verb stays indicative (-u).
Is it a sentence without a verb (X is Y / X is here / I have)? → لَيْسَ, agreeing with the subject (لَسْتُ، لَيْسَتْ …); with عِنْدَ always لَيْسَ.
After لَيْسَ, is there a noun or adjective predicate? → accusative (شَايًا، مُعَلِّمًا).
Do I mean “not … anything / anybody”? → negate the verb and add شَيْئًا / أَحَدًا; as an answer or subject: لَا شَيْءَ، لَا أَحَدَ.
Do I mean “never”? → لَا + verb … أَبَدًا.
Two things denied? → the normal negation first, then وَلَا before the second.
Is it past or future? → لَمْ + jussive / لَنْ + subjunctive — not لَا (later lessons).
Is it the answer “no”? → لَا on its own, then a comma: لَا، شُكْرًا.

traps: *لَا هٰذَا شَايٌ is wrong: a sentence without a verb takes لَيْسَ — هٰذَا لَيْسَ شَايًا.
*لَا عِنْدِي is wrong: عِنْدِي is not a verb — لَيْسَ عِنْدِي.
لَيْسَ looks like a past verb but means the present: لَسْتُ مُعَلِّمًا = I am not a teacher.
Do not double the negation: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا (not *لَا أُرِيدُ لَا شَيْءَ).
أَبَدًا alone after a positive verb means “forever” (literary), not “never”: say لَا … أَبَدًا.
Do not negate a past verb with لَا: “I didn’t eat” = لَمْ آكُلْ.
لَا “no” and لَا “not” are written the same; the answer is followed by a pause or comma: لَا، شُكْرًا.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew splits like Arabic: לֹא before verbs, אֵין for “there is not / does not have” (אֵין לִי — compare لَيْسَ عِنْدِي), and כְּלוּם / אַף אֶחָד for nothing / nobody — but Hebrew doubles the negation (אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה כְּלוּם), Arabic does not.
German chooses between nicht and kein by the word negated (kein Wasser); Arabic chooses by tense and sentence type (لَا، لَيْسَ، لَمْ، لَنْ) and has no word for kein.
Chinese chooses 不 or 没 by aspect — a little like Arabic لَا (present) vs لَمْ (past); 没有 “not have” matches لَيْسَ عِنْدَ.
The negative of عِنْدِي is لَيْسَ عِنْدِي (lesson 6).

head: kind of sentence
negator
example
rows: لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ. — I don’t drink coffee.
هٰذَا لَيْسَ شَايًا. — This is not tea.
الْقَهْوَةُ لَيْسَتْ هُنَا. — The coffee isn’t here.
لَيْسَ عِنْدَنَا مَاءٌ. — We have no water.
لَا شَيْءَ هُنَا. لَا أَحَدَ هُنَا.
لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا. — I don’t want anything.
لَا آكُلُ اللَّحْمَ أَبَدًا. — I never eat meat.

say
blocks.caption: لَيْسَ “is not” conjugated like a past verb. Before a consonant ending the stem shortens to las-: لَسْتُ، لَسْنَا، لَسْنَ. (Two people: لَسْتُمَا، لَيْسَا، لَيْسَتَا — later.)

blocks.title: لَا for verbs, لَيْسَ for sentences without a verb.
blocks.text: لَا تَطْبُخُ (she doesn’t cook) — but هِيَ لَيْسَتْ هُنَا (she isn’t here). Since عِنْدِي is not a verb, “I don’t have” is لَيْسَ عِنْدِي, never *لَا عِنْدِي.

blocks.title: The predicate of لَيْسَ is accusative.
blocks.text: هٰذَا شَايٌ → هٰذَا لَيْسَ شَايًا; أَنَا مُعَلِّمٌ → لَسْتُ مُعَلِّمًا. But in لَيْسَ عِنْدِي مَاءٌ the water is the subject: it stays nominative.

items.title: one negation
points: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا — I don’t want anything
لَا أَحَدَ هُنَا — nobody is here

items.title: not a second negation
points: after a negated verb: شَيْئًا (anything), أَحَدًا (anyone) — plain indefinites

notes.text: Greek δεν θέλω τίποτα has the same shape as لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا — a negated verb + “thing” — but τίποτα is negative by itself (alone it means “nothing”); شَيْئًا is a plain “something”, and “nothing” alone is لَا شَيْءَ.
Russian я ничего не хочу negates twice (ни- and не); Arabic negates once: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا.
Spanish no quiero nada negates twice; Arabic once: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا.
English “I don’t want anything” is built exactly like لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا.
French ne … rien has two parts; Arabic needs only لَا before the verb: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا.

blocks.title: “No car”, “no water”.
blocks.text: Arabic has no word for “no / not any” before a noun. Negate the sentence: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ (I have no car), لَا أَشْرَبُ نَبِيذًا (I drink no wine). The لَا of “there is no …” with a bare noun in -a (لَا شَكَّ, لَا شَيْءَ, لَا أَحَدَ) is the same word, used in set phrases and in these two pronouns.

notes.text: German kein has no Arabic counterpart: negate the sentence — لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ (ich habe kein Auto).

blocks.text: Word order stays the same: put لَا right before the verb (الطِّفْلُ لَا يَأْكُلُ) and لَيْسَ at the start or after the subject (لَيْسَ عِنْدِي … / هٰذَا لَيْسَ …). أَبَدًا usually goes to the end.

quiz.why: A present verb is negated with لَا.
No verb → لَيْسَ, and its predicate is accusative (-an).
عِنْدَ is not a verb: negate the sentence with لَيْسَ; the water stays nominative.
لَيْسَ agrees with “I”: لَسْتُ; predicate accusative.
أَبَدًا means “never” only with a negated verb.
The normal negation, then وَلَا before the second item.
لَيْسَ agrees with a feminine subject: لَيْسَتْ.

notes.text: Turkish also has separate words for sentences without a verb — değil (öğretmen değilim ≈ لَسْتُ مُعَلِّمًا) and yok for “there is not / have not” (suyum yok ≈ لَيْسَ عِنْدِي مَاءٌ); verbs take the suffix -me-, where Arabic puts لَا before them.
Korean also has a separate “is not” (아니다: 학생이 아니에요 ≈ لَسْتُ طَالِبًا) and “there is not / have not” (없다); verbs take 안 in front, as Arabic verbs take لَا.
Marathi has a negative “is not”, नाही (तो इथे नाही ≈ هُوَ لَيْسَ هُنَا), as Arabic has لَيْسَ; but Marathi puts the negation after the verb, Arabic لَا before it.
Hindi uses नहीं before the verb in every kind of sentence (मैं चाय नहीं पीता; वह यहाँ नहीं है); Arabic chooses: لَا for verbs, لَيْسَ for sentences without a verb.
Persian negates with a prefix on the verb (نمی‌خورم, I don’t eat; نیست, is not); Arabic uses separate words: لَا آكُلُ, لَيْسَ.
Japanese negates with an ending (食べない; 学生じゃない); Arabic with a word before the verb (لَا آكُلُ) or the verb لَيْسَ (لَسْتُ طَالِبًا).
Finnish negates with a verb that takes person endings (en, et, ei …); Arabic لَيْسَ is also a negative verb with person endings (لَسْتُ, لَسْتَ, لَيْسَ) — but only for sentences without another verb.
Hungarian has nincs for “there is not / have not” (nincs autóm), where Arabic says لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ; verbs take nem in front, like لَا.
Swahili also has a negative “is not”, si (mimi si mwalimu ≈ لَسْتُ مُعَلِّمًا), and negates verbs with prefixes (sili, I don’t eat); Arabic puts لَا before the verb.
Luganda negates verbs with a prefix (te- / si-); Arabic puts the word لَا before the verb, and uses the verb لَيْسَ for sentences without a verb.
Vietnamese không before the verb works like لَا (tôi không uống trà ≈ لَا أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ); for “is not” with a noun it says không phải là, where Arabic uses لَيْسَ.
Inuktitut negates with a suffix inside the verb (-nngit-); Arabic puts a separate word before the verb (لَا) or uses the verb لَيْسَ.
